faq.q: What is the difference between a secret and a surprise?
faq.a: A surprise is happy and is told soon, like a birthday gift. An unsafe secret makes you worried and someone wants it kept forever. Surprises are fine; worrying secrets must be told.
asks: Is it okay to keep a secret?

faq.q: What do I do if someone asks me to keep a worrying secret?
faq.a: Tell a trusted adult, like a parent, carer, teacher or grandparent, straight away. Even if they said or else, telling is the right thing.
asks: What if someone tells me not to tell?
Tell me about the Unsafe secret

faq.q: Will I get in trouble for telling a secret?
faq.a: No. You will never be in trouble for telling a trusted adult about a secret that worries you.
asks: What if telling gets me in trouble?

faq.q: What if a grown-up asks me to keep a secret?
faq.a: Safe grown-ups do not ask children to keep secrets from their parents or carers. If one does, tell another trusted adult.
asks: Can adults ask me to keep secrets?

faq.q: Can I keep a friend's small secret?
faq.a: Small, happy things, like who they like, are okay to keep. But if a secret means someone could get hurt, tell a trusted adult.
asks: Should I keep my friend's secret?

facts: Child-safety programmes teach children to keep surprises but to tell a trusted adult about any secret that makes them feel worried.
The NSPCC PANTS rule includes "Talk about secrets that upset you".
